paras: The lynching of Tom Tarver (also reported as Tom Carver and Tom Turner) took place in Dalton, Georgia, on the night of August 19, 1885, when about fifty masked "Regulators" raided houses they called disreputable, whipped several Black and white residents, and killed Tarver, a Black man. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of unknown parties, and no arrests were reported. The raid ran nationally under "Ku Klux" headlines, with sharply different accounts of how Tarver died.

A Dalton correspondent of the Savannah Morning News wrote that "lawlessness and disorder" had prevailed, that thieves and "lewd houses" had accumulated, and that the town had been "in a state of terror for a month" over burglaries and tramps.

Shortly after midnight about fifty disguised men entered the town; their notice was dated "Owl Hollow, Aug. 19, 1885," and the Dalton and Atlanta reports said they came from Murray County. At the boarding house of Ormstead McKain, described as "colored," they whipped McKain, his wife and a Black boarder; the Chattanooga wire said a man it called Armstead "will die," while a Memphis special said Armistead was only slightly wounded.

The band next went to the house of Thomas Tarver, a Black man who kept what the correspondent called "a disreputable house near the Baptist College." By the local account Tarver resisted being taken out to be whipped and was killed by a pistol ball in the back of the head and a crushing blow.

At the house of Mrs. Kidd, a white woman, the band fired about twenty shots after her son Bill, who fired and fled, then tore up the house and ordered her out of the city. It also wrecked the house of Lizzie Wilson, a white woman said to keep a house "for the benefit of negroes," and whipped her. Finally the band called out Mayor Samuel P. Maddox, demanded stricter enforcement of the laws, and left a list of people ordered to leave. The notice named "Tom Taryver and son John" among those "all colored" who must go, warned the McCains and "old Mrs. Kidd" against keeping white boarders, and threatened that thieves would be "taken out and hung without ceremony."

A coroner's jury held an inquest the next morning and returned a verdict of death at the hands of unknown parties. The correspondent reported "great regret" at Tarver's death and said an indignation meeting might be called, but on August 23 he wrote that those ordered out had left. The Marietta Journal complained that the Governor had been "dilatory," and no report of arrests appears in the coverage. On August 31 a Chattanooga dispatch said the same regulators had since whipped a man named Perry in Murray County.

A Chattanooga special to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, with fifty lashes and a half hour of torture, ran in the New-York Tribune, the Richmond Dispatch and papers as far off as Nevada, while an Atlanta version named the dead man Tom Turner and called the affair "an effort to rid Dalton of the bad characters that infest the town." Headlines ranged from "A Murderous Mob's Mad Doings" in the Richmond Dispatch to "Good Work by Ku Klux" in the St. Paul Daily Globe.

The Savannah Morning News headed its local letter "The Bad Elements of the City Roughly Handled," called Tarver "a corruptor of the race to which he belonged," and stressed that evil-doers "whether white or black" were punished alike. The Marietta Journal instead called the raid "a very unfortunate and disgraceful affair" and urged the Governor to have the maskers "ferreted out and punished." All coverage found came from white papers; no account was found in the Black press.

Where the Chattanooga wire said Tarver was tortured and beaten to death, the first Dalton letter, which reported the inquest, and the Memphis special said he was shot while resisting. A later Dalton letter, citing an unnamed eyewitness and remarks overheard from band members, said he attacked the band with an ax and ignored orders to "put down the ax" before being shot in the back. The Marietta Journal accepted the ax story but called him a man "who had acted only on the defensive."

framing.detail: Most papers ran one of two wires; headlines ranged from 'A Murderous Mob's Mad Doings' (Richmond) to 'Good Work by Ku Klux' (St. Paul).

The Savannah Morning News headed its local letter 'The Bad Elements of the City Roughly Handled' and called Tarver 'a corruptor of the race to which he belonged,' then printed an account blaming his death on his own ax attack.
The Sun headlined 'Ku-Klux Punishing Evil Doers' but reported that some residents were 'quite indignant.'
The Marietta Journal called it 'a very unfortunate and disgraceful affair' and urged the Governor to have the maskers punished.
